title: When the Zaps become the system
summary: Keep the Zaps when a person can explain each one and the tools agree on the records. If nobody can, the Zaps are now the system.
body_markdown:
You can keep the tools that already finish the job. Most owners we talk with are not shopping for new software. They want the tools they already pay for to hand the work to each other without a person in the middle. We help owners, ops managers, and the people who do the work see which automations to keep. Byte Bot is based in Clearwater, Florida. We work with blue collar teams in the Tampa Bay area and beyond.


This page is for a blue collar team that runs several products and connects them with Zapier or Make. Make is the automation product at make.com. The useful question is whether that glue is still helping, or whether the Zaps have become the system.


## When is business process automation still enough?


Stay with the products you rent when they can finish the job. If a standard product can do the job, we will recommend it. Our[About page](https://bytebot.io/about#about-honesty) says the same thing. Plenty of good businesses have run for years on a few Zaps that the team understands.


Stay on the rented tools when these are true:


Stay when the products can finish the job


- A person on the team can say what each automation does.
- You can turn one off, and you know what else it touches.
- The tools agree on the records that matter, or you already know which copy wins.
- A failed run is rare. When one fails, a named person knows the next step.
- The odd steps are habits. They are not how you win the work or keep a promise to a customer.


Business process automation is still the right help when it carries a fact from one product to the next. A person on the team can explain the rule. The automation is a helper. It is not the only place where the work is recorded.


If that list does not match your week, and someone is always fixing a Zap, the signs below will look familiar.


## What are the signs that the Zaps are now the system?


The Zaps have become the system when the company cannot finish the work without them, and nobody can see the whole path.


Signs the glue is now the system


- Nobody knows what a Zap does. The name in the list does not match a job anyone can describe.
- People are afraid to turn one off. They do not know what else depends on it.
- The data disagrees between tools. A job is done in one product and open in another. A payment is in one place and not in the books.
- Someone is babysitting failed runs. Checking the errors is part of that person’s week, and the team treats it as normal work.


One forgotten automation is a cleanup. A web of them, with fear and records that disagree, means the glue is now how the company runs.


Here is an illustrative example. It is not a result from a client project. A technician marks a job complete in the field app. A Zap sends that update to the office. Some mornings it does not.


The office keeps a notebook of the jobs that never arrived. Now the notebook is the record that people trust, not the Zap.


## What should you do with an inherited Zapier account?


First, learn who has access. Then record what each Zap does before you change anything.


An inherited Zapier account is the company login that stays after the person who built the automations leaves. Opening the account is not the same as knowing what each Zap does. The login stays. The knowledge often leaves with the person.


Record these first


- Who has access today.
- Which email gets the password reset, and which card pays the bill.
- Which steps the people who do the work trust, and which steps they redo by hand.


Do not turn the account off to feel safer. Let it run while you[record what each automation seems to do](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/8496291148685) . Sit with the person who fixes the failures, and have them show you one normal day. Include the workarounds.


If you cannot say what a Zap does, record it as a gap. A gap that you can see is safer than a guess. Use the same steps for a Make account that you inherited. If the person who built a whole system is gone, read[When the person who built your software is gone](https://bytebot.io/articles/when-your-developer-is-gone) .


## Is Make vs Zapier the choice that matters?


Make vs Zapier is often the wrong first choice. Neither product decides which record is true.


Would moving everything to Make fix it? Usually not by itself.


Both products[wait for an event in one tool](https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/8496309697421) . Then they send a fact to another tool. One of them may offer a step that the other does not. A lower bill, or a step you cannot build today, can be a fair reason to move that one step. The move does not, by itself, make the handoffs clear.


Zapier alternatives in that same family have the same limit. They connect products. They do not decide which record is true. If two tools disagree, a new connector moves the disagreement faster.


Change products when you need a feature, a price, or access you do not have. Stay when the problem is that nobody can explain the path. Rebuilding the same Zaps in a new product only copies the confusion. A new set of automations can hide that problem for a while.


## What should you do when the automations are not enough?


Test one real job before you add another connector. Adding a connector rarely fixes a path that nobody can explain. The test shows if any part of that job is worth the cost to own.


You can find the steps of that test in[our guide on when to own a system](https://bytebot.io/articles/when-custom-software-is-worth-owning) . A low price to write code is not a reason to start. We explain why in[our article on the lower cost of code](https://bytebot.io/articles/building-software-just-got-cheap) .


## What can you do before you replace anything?


You can make one path visible before you pay to replace it.


Pick one job the company cares about. A sold job, a service call, or an invoice is enough. Write the steps from the first record to the last. For each automation on that path, write its name, what you think it does, and who fixes it when it fails. Where two tools disagree, write which copy the team trusts today.


Writing it all on one page is often the first time anyone sees the whole path.


Bring that page to a conversation. You do not need a plan. The first conversation is free, and we will tell you if we are a fit.[Schedule a conversation](https://bytebot.io/schedule?meeting=intro) .

## Questions people ask


### Should we stay on the rented tools if most of the Zaps work?


Yes, when three things are true. A person can explain each automation. The tools agree on the records that matter. You can change one automation without fear. If a standard product can do the job, we recommend it.


### What are the signs that the Zaps are now the system?


Nobody can say what a Zap does. People are afraid to turn one off. The same fact disagrees between tools. Someone is babysitting the failed runs. One old automation is a cleanup. A set of these signs means the Zaps have become the system.


### Is Make vs Zapier a way out?


Only when you need a feature, a price, or access that the current product does not give you. Make vs Zapier does not decide which record is true. Zapier alternatives that only connect other products have the same limit.


### What is an inherited Zapier account?


It is the company Zapier login that stays after the person who built the automations leaves. You can open the account, but that does not tell you what each Zap does.
